Triangles

Angle sum

A+B+C=180∘A + B + C = 180^\circA+B+C=180∘

Symbols: AAA, BBB, CCC: the three angles of the triangle.

The idea

Draw the line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side: the three angles of the triangle reappear along that line as alternate angles, and together they make a straight angle, 180°180°180°.

Worked example

A=50°A = 50°A=50°, B=60°B = 60°B=60°: C=180°−110°=70°C = 180° - 110° = 70°C=180°−110°=70°.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Area

S=12 c h=12 absin⁡CS = \tfrac12\,c\,h = \tfrac12\,ab\sin CS=21​ch=21​absinC

Symbols: aaa, bbb, ccc: the sides opposite AAA, BBB, CCC; hhh: the height onto side ccc; SSS: the area.

The idea

Half of base times height: the triangle is half of the rectangle around it. If you know two sides and the angle between them, the height on side aaa is bsin⁡Cb\sin CbsinC, which gives 12absin⁡C\tfrac12 ab\sin C21​absinC.

Worked example

Base 8 and height 5: S=20S = 20S=20. Sides 6 and 8 with 30°30°30° between them: S=12⋅6⋅8⋅12=12S = \tfrac12\cdot 6\cdot 8\cdot\tfrac12 = 12S=21​⋅6⋅8⋅21​=12.

Heron’s formula

S=s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c),s=a+b+c2S = \sqrt{s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)}, \quad s = \frac{a + b + c}{2}S=s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)​,s=2a+b+c​

sss is the semi-perimeter: half of the perimeter a+b+ca + b + ca+b+c. Area from the three sides alone, no height or angle needed.

The idea

Heron gives the area of a triangle from its three sides alone — no height, no angle. First compute the semi-perimeter sss: half of the perimeter, s=a+b+c2s = \tfrac{a + b + c}{2}s=2a+b+c​. Then subtract each side from sss, multiply the four numbers sss, s−as - as−a, s−bs - bs−b, s−cs - cs−c, and take the square root. Each s−as - as−a is positive because one side is always shorter than the other two together.

Worked example

Sides 555, 666, 777: the perimeter is 181818, so s=9s = 9s=9. Then s−a=4s - a = 4s−a=4, s−b=3s - b = 3s−b=3, s−c=2s - c = 2s−c=2, and S=9⋅4⋅3⋅2=216=66≈14.7S = \sqrt{9\cdot 4\cdot 3\cdot 2} = \sqrt{216} = 6\sqrt6 \approx 14.7S=9⋅4⋅3⋅2​=216​=66​≈14.7.

Sides 5,6,75, 6, 75,6,7: s=9s = 9s=9, S=9⋅4⋅3⋅2=216=66S = \sqrt{9\cdot 4\cdot 3\cdot 2} = \sqrt{216} = 6\sqrt6S=9⋅4⋅3⋅2​=216​=66​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Triangle inequality

∣a−b∣<c<a+b|a - b| < c < a + b∣a−b∣<c<a+b

The idea

The straight path is the shortest, so each side is shorter than the other two together. With three lengths, check only that the longest is less than the sum of the other two. For a missing side: ∣a−b∣<c<a+b\lvert a - b\rvert < c < a + b∣a−b∣<c<a+b.

Worked example

Sticks 3, 4 and 8: 3+4=7<83 + 4 = 7 < 83+4=7<8, so they cannot close up (the picture). Sticks 3, 4, 6: 3+4>63 + 4 > 63+4>6, so they form a triangle.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Exterior angle

180∘−C=A+B180^\circ - C = A + B180∘−C=A+B

The idea

Extend one side: the exterior angle and the interior angle CCC make 180°180°180°, and so do A+B+CA + B + CA+B+C. So the exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.

Worked example

A=45°A = 45°A=45° and B=65°B = 65°B=65°: the exterior angle at CCC is 110°110°110° — no need to find C=70°C = 70°C=70° first.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Largest side

a>b  ⟺  A>Ba > b \iff A > Ba>b⟺A>B

The largest side faces the largest angle.

The idea

In a triangle the longer side faces the larger angle, and vice versa: open the angle wider and the opposite side stretches. So to order the sides, order the angles.

Worked example

Sides a=7a = 7a=7, b=5b = 5b=5, c=6c = 6c=6: the largest angle is AAA (opposite 7), the smallest is BBB (opposite 5).

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Right triangles

Pythagoras

a2+b2=c2a^2 + b^2 = c^2a2+b2=c2

Symbols: aaa, bbb: the legs (the sides at the right angle), ccc: the hypotenuse.

The idea

In a right triangle, the square on the hypotenuse has the same area as the squares on the two legs together. Use it to find a missing side, and backwards: if a2+b2=c2a^2 + b^2 = c^2a2+b2=c2, the angle opposite ccc is right.

Worked example

Legs 6 and 8: c=36+64=10c = \sqrt{36 + 64} = 10c=36+64​=10.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Altitude to the hypotenuse

h=abch = \frac{ab}{c}h=cab​h2=p qh^2 = p\,qh2=pq

p,qp, qp,q: the pieces of the hypotenuse.

Symbols: hhh: the height from the right angle to the hypotenuse ccc.

The idea

The area can be written with the legs (12ab\tfrac12 ab21​ab) or with the hypotenuse and its altitude (12ch\tfrac12 ch21​ch), so h=abch = \tfrac{ab}{c}h=cab​. The altitude splits the triangle into two triangles similar to it, which gives h2=pqh^2 = pqh2=pq with ppp, qqq the pieces of the hypotenuse.

Worked example

Legs 6 and 8, hypotenuse 10: h=4810=4.8h = \tfrac{48}{10} = 4.8h=1048​=4.8. The pieces are p=3.6p = 3.6p=3.6 and q=6.4q = 6.4q=6.4, and indeed 3.6⋅6.4=23.04=4.823.6\cdot 6.4 = 23.04 = 4.8^23.6⋅6.4=23.04=4.82.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Legs and projections

a2=c pa^2 = c\,pa2=cpb2=c qb^2 = c\,qb2=cq

Symbols: ppp, qqq: the pieces of the hypotenuse next to aaa and bbb (their projections).

The idea

Each leg is the mean proportional between the hypotenuse and its own projection on it (Euclid’s leg theorem). It comes from the same similar triangles: ac=pa\tfrac{a}{c} = \tfrac{p}{a}ca​=ap​.

Worked example

Hypotenuse 10, leg 6: its projection is p=3610=3.6p = \tfrac{36}{10} = 3.6p=1036​=3.6; the other leg’s projection is 10−3.6=6.410 - 3.6 = 6.410−3.6=6.4, and 82=10⋅6.48^2 = 10\cdot 6.482=10⋅6.4.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Median to the hypotenuse

mc=c2m_c = \frac c2mc​=2c​

The hypotenuse is a diameter of the circumcircle.

Symbols: mcm_cmc​: the median from the right angle to the midpoint of the hypotenuse.

The idea

A right triangle is half of a rectangle; its hypotenuse is a diagonal, and the diagonals of a rectangle bisect each other and are equal. So the midpoint of the hypotenuse is equally far from all three vertices — the circumcentre — and mc=c2m_c = \tfrac c2mc​=2c​.

Worked example

Legs 6 and 8, hypotenuse 10: the median from the right angle is 5, and the circle through the three vertices has the hypotenuse as diameter.

Special triangles

30∘ ⁣− ⁣60∘ ⁣− ⁣90∘: 1:3:230^\circ\!-\!60^\circ\!-\!90^\circ:\ 1 : \sqrt3 : 230∘−60∘−90∘: 1:3​:245∘ ⁣− ⁣45∘ ⁣− ⁣90∘: 1:1:245^\circ\!-\!45^\circ\!-\!90^\circ:\ 1 : 1 : \sqrt245∘−45∘−90∘: 1:1:2​

The idea

Half an equilateral triangle is a 30°30°30°–60°60°60°–90°90°90° triangle with sides 1:3:21 : \sqrt3 : 21:3​:2; half a square is a 45°45°45°–45°45°45°–90°90°90° triangle with sides 1:1:21 : 1 : \sqrt21:1:2​. They give the exact values of sin, cos and tan at 30°30°30°, 45°45°45°, 60°60°60°.

Worked example

A 30°30°30°–60°60°60°–90°90°90° triangle with hypotenuse 10: the short leg (opposite 30°30°30°) is 5, the long leg 53≈8.665\sqrt3 \approx 8.6653​≈8.66.

Pythagorean triples

(3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17), (7,24,25)(3, 4, 5),\ (5, 12, 13),\ (8, 15, 17),\ (7, 24, 25)(3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17), (7,24,25)

The idea

Whole-number right triangles. Multiples of a triple are triples (6,8,106, 8, 106,8,10), and every primitive triple comes from two numbers m>nm > nm>n: (m2−n2, 2mn, m2+n2)(m^2 - n^2,\ 2mn,\ m^2 + n^2)(m2−n2, 2mn, m2+n2). Recognising them saves square roots.

Worked example

m=4m = 4m=4, n=1n = 1n=1: (15,8,17)(15, 8, 17)(15,8,17); check 225+64=289=172225 + 64 = 289 = 17^2225+64=289=172.

Centres and special lines

Circumradius

R=abc4S=a2sin⁡AR = \frac{abc}{4S} = \frac{a}{2\sin A}R=4Sabc​=2sinAa​

Symbols: RRR: radius of the circle through the three vertices; SSS: the area; aaa, bbb, ccc: the sides.

The idea

The circle through the three vertices has its centre where the perpendicular bisectors meet. Its radius follows from the extended law of sines, asin⁡A=2R\tfrac{a}{\sin A} = 2RsinAa​=2R, or from the area, R=abc4SR = \tfrac{abc}{4S}R=4Sabc​.

Worked example

For 3-4-5: R=604⋅6=2.5R = \tfrac{60}{4\cdot 6} = 2.5R=4⋅660​=2.5 — half the hypotenuse, as expected. For 13-14-15 (S=84S = 84S=84): R=2730336=8.125R = \tfrac{2730}{336} = 8.125R=3362730​=8.125.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Inradius

r=Ssr = \frac{S}{s}r=sS​

sss is the semiperimeter.

Symbols: rrr: radius of the circle inside touching all three sides; SSS: the area.

The idea

Join the incentre III to the three vertices: the triangle splits into three triangles, each with height rrr and one side as base. Their areas add up to 12r(a+b+c)=r s\tfrac12 r(a + b + c) = r\,s21​r(a+b+c)=rs, where sss is the semi-perimeter (half of the perimeter). So S=rsS = rsS=rs and r=Ssr = \tfrac Ssr=sS​.

Worked example

The 3-4-5 right triangle: S=12⋅3⋅4=6S = \tfrac12\cdot 3\cdot 4 = 6S=21​⋅3⋅4=6 and s=3+4+52=6s = \tfrac{3 + 4 + 5}{2} = 6s=23+4+5​=6, so r=1r = 1r=1. The picture shows the circle of radius 1 touching all three sides.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Median length

ma=122b2+2c2−a2m_a = \tfrac12\sqrt{2b^2 + 2c^2 - a^2}ma​=21​2b2+2c2−a2​

Symbols: mam_ama​: the median from AAA to the midpoint of side aaa.

The idea

The median from AAA goes to the midpoint of aaa. Apollonius: b2+c2=2ma2+a22b^2 + c^2 = 2m_a^2 + \tfrac{a^2}{2}b2+c2=2ma2​+2a2​ (the parallelogram law, since doubling the median gives a parallelogram with sides bbb, ccc and diagonals aaa, 2ma2m_a2ma​). Solve for mam_ama​.

Worked example

Sides 7, 8, 9, median to the side 8: 122⋅49+2⋅81−64=12196=7\tfrac12\sqrt{2\cdot 49 + 2\cdot 81 - 64} = \tfrac12\sqrt{196} = 721​2⋅49+2⋅81−64​=21​196​=7.

Centroid

AG:GM=2:1AG : GM = 2 : 1AG:GM=2:1

Symbols: GGG: the centroid, MMM: the midpoint of the side opposite AAA.

The idea

The three medians meet at one point GGG, two thirds of the way from each vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. So AGAGAG is twice GMGMGM, and AG=23AG = \tfrac23AG=32​ of the median.

Worked example

A median of length 9 is cut by GGG into AG=6AG = 6AG=6 and GM=3GM = 3GM=3.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Angle bisector theorem

BDDC=ABAC\frac{BD}{DC} = \frac{AB}{AC}DCBD​=ACAB​

Symbols: ADADAD: the bisector of angle AAA, with DDD on side BCBCBC.

The idea

The bisector of angle AAA cuts the opposite side in the same ratio as the two adjacent sides. The two small triangles have the same height from AAA, and their areas are also 12⋅AB⋅ADsin⁡A2\tfrac12\cdot AB\cdot AD\sin\tfrac A221​⋅AB⋅ADsin2A​ and 12⋅AC⋅ADsin⁡A2\tfrac12\cdot AC\cdot AD\sin\tfrac A221​⋅AC⋅ADsin2A​.

Worked example

AB=6AB = 6AB=6, AC=9AC = 9AC=9, BC=10BC = 10BC=10: the bisector from AAA splits BCBCBC in the ratio 2:32 : 32:3, so BD=4BD = 4BD=4 and DC=6DC = 6DC=6.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Similar triangles

L′=kL,S′=k2S,V′=k3VL' = kL, \quad S' = k^2 S, \quad V' = k^3 VL′=kL,S′=k2S,V′=k3V

Lengths scale by k, areas by k², volumes by k³.

Symbols: kkk: the similarity ratio; LLL, SSS, VVV: a length, an area, a volume.

The idea

If every length is multiplied by kkk, areas are multiplied by k2k^2k2 (two directions) and volumes by k3k^3k3 (three directions). Angles do not change. Doubling a model makes it four times the paint and eight times the weight.

Worked example

Scale factor k=3k = 3k=3: a triangle of area 5 becomes area 454545; a box of volume 2 becomes volume 545454.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Circles

Circumference and area

C=2πrC = 2\pi rC=2πrS=πr2S = \pi r^2S=πr2

Symbols: rrr: the radius, CCC: the circumference, SSS: the area.

The idea

π\piπ is the ratio of circumference to diameter, so C=2πrC = 2\pi rC=2πr. Cut the disc into thin sectors and lay them alternately: they form almost a rectangle of width πr\pi rπr (half the circumference) and height rrr, so S=πr2S = \pi r^2S=πr2.

Worked example

r=3r = 3r=3: C=6π≈18.85C = 6\pi \approx 18.85C=6π≈18.85 and S=9π≈28.27S = 9\pi \approx 28.27S=9π≈28.27.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Arc length

s=rθs = r\thetas=rθ

θ\thetaθ in radians.

Symbols: sss: the arc length, rrr: the radius, θ\thetaθ: the central angle.

The idea

An angle of one radian cuts off an arc as long as the radius — that is the definition of the radian. So an angle of θ\thetaθ radians cuts off θ\thetaθ radii: s=rθs = r\thetas=rθ. In degrees: s=α360⋅2πrs = \tfrac{\alpha}{360}\cdot 2\pi rs=360α​⋅2πr.

Worked example

r=5r = 5r=5, θ=1.2\theta = 1.2θ=1.2 rad: s=6s = 6s=6.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Sector area

S=12r2θ=12rsS = \tfrac12 r^2\theta = \tfrac12 r sS=21​r2θ=21​rs

Symbols: θ\thetaθ: the central angle in radians, sss: the arc length.

The idea

A sector is the fraction θ2π\tfrac{\theta}{2\pi}2πθ​ of the disc: θ2π⋅πr2=12r2θ\tfrac{\theta}{2\pi}\cdot\pi r^2 = \tfrac12 r^2\theta2πθ​⋅πr2=21​r2θ. Since s=rθs = r\thetas=rθ, this is also 12rs\tfrac12 rs21​rs — like a triangle with base sss and height rrr.

Worked example

r=4r = 4r=4, θ=π3\theta = \tfrac\pi3θ=3π​: S=12⋅16⋅π3=8π3≈8.38S = \tfrac12\cdot 16\cdot\tfrac\pi3 = \tfrac{8\pi}{3} \approx 8.38S=21​⋅16⋅3π​=38π​≈8.38.

Degrees and radians

180∘=π rad180^\circ = \pi \text{ rad}180∘=π radθ=π α∘180\theta = \frac{\pi\,\alpha^\circ}{180}θ=180πα∘​

Symbols: α∘\alpha^\circα∘: the angle in degrees, θ\thetaθ: the same angle in radians.

The idea

A full turn is 360°360°360° or 2π2\pi2π radians, so 180°=π180° = \pi180°=π. To convert degrees to radians multiply by π180\tfrac{\pi}{180}180π​; the other way, by 180π\tfrac{180}{\pi}π180​. One radian is about 57.3°57.3°57.3°.

Worked example

135°=135π180=3π4135° = \tfrac{135\pi}{180} = \tfrac{3\pi}{4}135°=180135π​=43π​, and 222 rad =360°π≈114.6°= \tfrac{360°}{\pi} \approx 114.6°=π360°​≈114.6°.

Chord

AB=2rsin⁡θ2AB = 2r\sin\frac\theta2AB=2rsin2θ​

Symbols: θ\thetaθ: the central angle that the chord ABABAB subtends; rrr: the radius.

The idea

The radius perpendicular to a chord bisects it and bisects the central angle. Each half-chord is the side opposite θ2\tfrac\theta22θ​ in a right triangle with hypotenuse rrr: AB2=rsin⁡θ2\tfrac{AB}{2} = r\sin\tfrac\theta22AB​=rsin2θ​.

Worked example

r=10r = 10r=10, θ=60°\theta = 60°θ=60°: AB=2⋅10⋅sin⁡30°=10AB = 2\cdot 10\cdot\sin 30° = 10AB=2⋅10⋅sin30°=10 — the chord equals the radius (an equilateral triangle).

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Segment area

S=12r2(θ−sin⁡θ)S = \tfrac12 r^2(\theta - \sin\theta)S=21​r2(θ−sinθ)

Symbols: θ\thetaθ: the central angle in radians; the segment lies between the chord and the arc.

The idea

A segment is the part of a sector beyond its chord: sector minus the isosceles triangle. The triangle has two sides rrr and angle θ\thetaθ, area 12r2sin⁡θ\tfrac12 r^2\sin\theta21​r2sinθ. Hence 12r2(θ−sin⁡θ)\tfrac12 r^2(\theta - \sin\theta)21​r2(θ−sinθ) — with θ\thetaθ in radians.

Worked example

r=6r = 6r=6, θ=π3\theta = \tfrac\pi3θ=3π​: 12⋅36(π3−32)=6π−93≈3.26\tfrac12\cdot 36\left(\tfrac\pi3 - \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right) = 6\pi - 9\sqrt3 \approx 3.2621​⋅36(3π​−23​​)=6π−93​≈3.26.

Circle theorems

Inscribed angle

∠APB=12 ∠AOB\angle APB = \tfrac12\,\angle AOB∠APB=21​∠AOB

Symbols: OOO: the centre, PPP: a point on the circle, AAA, BBB: the ends of the arc.

The idea

An angle with its vertex on the circle is half the central angle on the same arc. So all inscribed angles on the same arc are equal, wherever PPP sits on the major arc.

Worked example

A central angle of 100°100°100°: every inscribed angle on that arc is 50°50°50°.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Angle in a semicircle

AB=2r ⇒ ∠APB=90∘AB = 2r \ \Rightarrow\ \angle APB = 90^\circAB=2r ⇒ ∠APB=90∘

The idea

When ABABAB is a diameter, the central angle is 180°180°180°, so the inscribed angle is 90°90°90° (Thales). Any triangle drawn on a diameter with its third vertex on the circle is right-angled — Pythagoras applies.

Worked example

Diameter 13 and chord PA=5PA = 5PA=5: the triangle is right-angled at PPP, so PB=169−25=12PB = \sqrt{169 - 25} = 12PB=169−25​=12.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Cyclic quadrilateral

A+C=B+D=180∘A + C = B + D = 180^\circA+C=B+D=180∘

Symbols: AAA, BBB, CCC, DDD: the angles of a quadrilateral whose vertices lie on a circle.

The idea

If the four vertices lie on a circle, opposite angles stand on arcs that make up the whole circle; their central angles add to 360°360°360°, so the angles add to 180°180°180°. Conversely, opposite angles adding to 180°180°180° means the quadrilateral is cyclic.

Worked example

A=80°A = 80°A=80°: the opposite angle C=100°C = 100°C=100°.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Tangent and radius

OT⊥tOT \perp tOT⊥t

The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.

Symbols: OOO: the centre, TTT: the point of contact, ttt: the tangent line.

The idea

The tangent touches the circle at one point TTT, and there it is perpendicular to the radius OTOTOT. So OOO, TTT and an outside point PPP form a right triangle with hypotenuse OPOPOP: PT2=OP2−r2PT^2 = OP^2 - r^2PT2=OP2−r2.

Worked example

r=5r = 5r=5 and OP=13OP = 13OP=13: the tangent from PPP has length 169−25=12\sqrt{169 - 25} = 12169−25​=12.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Equal tangents

PT1=PT2PT_1 = PT_2PT1​=PT2​

Two tangents from an outside point have equal length.

Symbols: PPP: the outside point, T1T_1T1​, T2T_2T2​: the two points of contact.

The idea

The two tangents from an outside point are equally long: the right triangles OPT1OPT_1OPT1​ and OPT2OPT_2OPT2​ share the hypotenuse OPOPOP and have equal legs rrr. Consequence for a quadrilateral around a circle: opposite sides have equal sums (Pitot).

Worked example

A quadrilateral around a circle: each vertex sends two equal tangent pieces, so AB+CD=BC+DAAB + CD = BC + DAAB+CD=BC+DA. With AB=7AB = 7AB=7, BC=6BC = 6BC=6, CD=9CD = 9CD=9: DA=10DA = 10DA=10.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Power of a point

PA⋅PB=PC⋅PD=PT2PA\cdot PB = PC\cdot PD = PT^2PA⋅PB=PC⋅PD=PT2

Symbols: Two lines through PPP cut the circle at A,BA, BA,B and at C,DC, DC,D; PTPTPT: a tangent from PPP.

The idea

Through a point PPP draw any line meeting the circle at AAA and BBB: the product PA⋅PBPA\cdot PBPA⋅PB is the same for every line (similar triangles). For a tangent the two points merge into TTT, giving PT2PT^2PT2. It works for chords crossing inside the circle too.

Worked example

PA=4PA = 4PA=4 and PB=9PB = 9PB=9 on a secant: the tangent from PPP has PT2=36PT^2 = 36PT2=36, so PT=6PT = 6PT=6.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Polygons and quadrilaterals

Interior angle sum

(n−2)⋅180∘(n - 2)\cdot180^\circ(n−2)⋅180∘

Symbols: nnn: the number of sides.

The idea

From one vertex, the diagonals cut an nnn-gon into n−2n - 2n−2 triangles, each contributing 180°180°180°. So the angles add to (n−2)⋅180°(n - 2)\cdot 180°(n−2)⋅180°: 360° for a quadrilateral, 540° for a pentagon…

Worked example

A hexagon splits into 4 triangles: 4⋅180°=720°4\cdot 180° = 720°4⋅180°=720°.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Regular polygon angle

(n−2)⋅180∘n\frac{(n - 2)\cdot180^\circ}{n}n(n−2)⋅180∘​

The exterior angles always add up to 360°.

The idea

In a regular polygon all angles are equal, so divide the sum by nnn. Easier: each exterior angle is 360°n\tfrac{360°}{n}n360°​ (walking round, you turn a full turn), and the interior angle is 180°180°180° minus that.

Worked example

Regular octagon: exterior 45°45°45°, interior 135°135°135°.

Diagonals

n(n−3)2\frac{n(n - 3)}{2}2n(n−3)​

The idea

Each vertex joins the n−3n - 3n−3 vertices that are not itself or its neighbours. That gives n(n−3)n(n - 3)n(n−3), but every diagonal was counted from both ends, so divide by 2.

Worked example

Octagon: 8⋅52=20\tfrac{8\cdot 5}{2} = 2028⋅5​=20 diagonals, all drawn in the picture.

Regular polygon area

S=12 P a=12 nR2sin⁡2πnS = \tfrac12\,P\,a = \tfrac12\,n R^2\sin\frac{2\pi}{n}S=21​Pa=21​nR2sinn2π​

PPP perimeter, aaa apothem, RRR circumradius.

The idea

Join the centre to the vertices: nnn equal isosceles triangles, each with two sides RRR and angle 2πn\tfrac{2\pi}{n}n2π​. Or use the apothem aaa (centre to side): each triangle is 12⋅side⋅a\tfrac12\cdot\text{side}\cdot a21​⋅side⋅a, so S=12PaS = \tfrac12 P aS=21​Pa.

Worked example

Regular hexagon with side 2 (so R=2R = 2R=2): S=12⋅6⋅4⋅sin⁡60°=63≈10.39S = \tfrac12\cdot 6\cdot 4\cdot\sin 60° = 6\sqrt3 \approx 10.39S=21​⋅6⋅4⋅sin60°=63​≈10.39 — six equilateral triangles of area 3\sqrt33​.

Parallelogram, rhombus, trapezoid

S=b hS = b\,hS=bhS=d1d22S = \frac{d_1 d_2}{2}S=2d1​d2​​S=(a+b) h2S = \frac{(a + b)\,h}{2}S=2(a+b)h​

Symbols: bbb: base, hhh: height, d1d_1d1​, d2d_2d2​: the diagonals, aaa, bbb: the two parallel sides of the trapezoid.

The idea

Slide a triangle from one end of a parallelogram to the other and you get a rectangle: bhbhbh. A rhombus is half of the rectangle built on its diagonals. Two copies of a trapezoid, one turned round, make a parallelogram of base a+ba + ba+b.

Worked example

Trapezoid with bases 5 and 9 and height 4: 14⋅42=28\tfrac{14\cdot 4}{2} = 28214⋅4​=28. Rhombus with diagonals 6 and 8: 242424.

Shoelace formula

S=12∣∑i(xiyi+1−xi+1yi)∣S = \tfrac12\left|\sum_{i} (x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i)\right|S=21​​i∑​(xi​yi+1​−xi+1​yi​)​

Symbols: (xi,yi)(x_i, y_i)(xi​,yi​): the vertices in order around the polygon; after the last one comes the first again.

The idea

List the vertices in order around the polygon (repeat the first at the end). Multiply crosswise, xiyi+1−xi+1yix_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_ixi​yi+1​−xi+1​yi​, add, halve, take the absolute value. It works for any simple polygon given by coordinates.

Worked example

(0,0),(4,0),(4,3),(0,5)(0, 0), (4, 0), (4, 3), (0, 5)(0,0),(4,0),(4,3),(0,5): 0+12+20+0=320 + 12 + 20 + 0 = 320+12+20+0=32, so S=16S = 16S=16 — a right trapezoid with bases 3 and 5 and height 4.

Solids

Cube and box

V=a3,d=a3;V = a^3, \quad d = a\sqrt3;V=a3,d=a3​;V=abc,d=a2+b2+c2V = abc, \quad d = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}V=abc,d=a2+b2+c2​

Symbols: aaa: the edge of the cube; aaa, bbb, ccc: the edges of the box; ddd: the space diagonal; VVV: volume.

The idea

Volume: length × width × height. The space diagonal uses Pythagoras twice — across the base, then up — so d=a2+b2+c2d = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}d=a2+b2+c2​; for a cube a3a\sqrt3a3​.

Worked example

A box 3×4×123 \times 4 \times 123×4×12: V=144V = 144V=144 and d=9+16+144=13d = \sqrt{9 + 16 + 144} = 13d=9+16+144​=13.

Prism and cylinder

V=B hV = B\,hV=BhV=πr2h,A=2πr(r+h)V = \pi r^2 h, \quad A = 2\pi r(r + h)V=πr2h,A=2πr(r+h)

Symbols: BBB: the area of the base, hhh: the height, rrr: the radius, AAA: the total surface area.

The idea

A prism or cylinder is a base pushed straight up: stack copies of the base hhh high, so V=BhV = BhV=Bh. The curved side of a cylinder unrolls into a rectangle 2πr2\pi r2πr by hhh; add the two discs for the total area.

Worked example

Cylinder r=3r = 3r=3, h=5h = 5h=5: V=45π≈141.4V = 45\pi \approx 141.4V=45π≈141.4 and A=2π⋅3⋅8=48πA = 2\pi\cdot 3\cdot 8 = 48\piA=2π⋅3⋅8=48π.

Pyramid and cone

V=13B hV = \tfrac13 B\,hV=31​BhV=13πr2h,Alat=πrlV = \tfrac13\pi r^2 h, \quad A_{\text{lat}} = \pi r lV=31​πr2h,Alat​=πrl

Slant height l=r2+h2l = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2}l=r2+h2​.

Symbols: BBB: the area of the base, hhh: the height, AlatA_{\text{lat}}Alat​: the lateral area.

The idea

A pyramid or cone holds exactly one third of the prism or cylinder with the same base and height (three square pyramids fit into a cube). The lateral surface of a cone unrolls into a sector of radius lll (the slant height) and arc 2πr2\pi r2πr, area πrl\pi r lπrl.

Worked example

Cone r=3r = 3r=3, h=4h = 4h=4: slant height l=5l = 5l=5, V=13π⋅9⋅4=12πV = \tfrac13\pi\cdot 9\cdot 4 = 12\piV=31​π⋅9⋅4=12π, lateral area 15π15\pi15π.

Sphere

V=43πr3V = \tfrac43\pi r^3V=34​πr3A=4πr2A = 4\pi r^2A=4πr2

The idea

Archimedes’ favourite result: a sphere fills two thirds of the cylinder around it, 23⋅πr2⋅2r=43πr3\tfrac23\cdot\pi r^2\cdot 2r = \tfrac43\pi r^332​⋅πr2⋅2r=34​πr3, and its surface equals the cylinder’s curved side, 2πr⋅2r=4πr22\pi r\cdot 2r = 4\pi r^22πr⋅2r=4πr2 — four great circles.

Worked example

r=3r = 3r=3: V=43π⋅27=36πV = \tfrac43\pi\cdot 27 = 36\piV=34​π⋅27=36π and A=4π⋅9=36πA = 4\pi\cdot 9 = 36\piA=4π⋅9=36π — equal numbers, but different units.

Euler’s formula

V−E+F=2V - E + F = 2V−E+F=2

Vertices, edges and faces of a convex polyhedron.

The idea

For any convex polyhedron, vertices minus edges plus faces is always 2. It is a quick check when counting, and it lets you find one of VVV, EEE, FFF from the other two.

Worked example

Cube: 8−12+6=28 - 12 + 6 = 28−12+6=2. Tetrahedron: 4−6+4=24 - 6 + 4 = 24−6+4=2. Octahedron: 6−12+8=26 - 12 + 8 = 26−12+8=2.
